name: Mon
confidence_why: 3 independent first-hand descriptions agree (2 state the same rule, 0 refine it); none contradicts.
catalog_citation: Huffman, Franklin E. 1990. Burmese Mon, Thai Mon, and Nyah Kur: a synchronic comparison. Mon-Khmer Studies 16-17: 31-84.
catalog_locator: p. 39, sec. 1.1.3 'Syllable Structure' (Burmese Mon); cf. p. 46, sec. 1.2.3 (Thai Mon)
catalog_quote: [p. 39] Burmese Mon phonological words consist either of a single stressed syllable of the structure /C(C)(C)V́(V)(C)/, or of such a syllable preceded by an unstressed presyllable of the structure /CV-/. In such presyllables the vowel is almost invariably /a/ (varying in quality between [a] and [ə]), with several occurrences of /ʔi-/; e.g.: /pasɔɲ/ [pᵃsɔ́ⁱɲ] ~ [pəsɔ́ⁱɲ] 'five' /ʔinae/ [ʔiʔná·ɛ] ~ [ʔiná·ɛ] 'aunt (FaOlSi)' Thus the syllable structure of Mon can be stated as (CV)C(C)(C)V́(V)(C), with /CV́/ as the minimal syllabic unit. ... [p. 46] The syllable structure of Thai Mon appears to be basically identical with that of Burmese Mon, i.e. (CV)C(C)(C)V́(V)(C), with /CV́/ being the minimal syllabic unit.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Mon (monn1252) is not in the catalog. All three title-works with stress in the title are Glottolog mis-links: Uwano 2006 (verified on CiNii: Gengo Kenkyu 130:1-42, DOI 10.11435/gengo.130.0_1) is a reconstruction of Japanese accent, and Koiso & Ishimoto 2012 / Ishimoto & Koiso 2012 are intonation-phrase studies on the Corpus of Spontaneous Japanese; none concerns Mon, priority none. Ferlus 1984 Essai de phonétique historique, pp.1-12) -- both silent on word stress. The material already held by the project from the 2026-09-17 check was re-read from page scan and gives four convergent first-hand statements: Huffman 1990 p.39 (word = one stressed syllable optionally preceded by an unstressed CV- presyllable; Thai Mon identical, p.46), Haswell/Stevens 1901 §12 pp.11-12 (accent on the second syllable of disyllables), Panthongkhum 1983 pp.17-20 (Bang Khanmak Thai Mon: non-phonemic; syllable 2 in disyllables, 1+3 in trisyllables, 2+4 in four-syllable strings) and Khonthet 1985 pp.46-48 (Chet Riu Thai Mon: minor disyllables stressed on syllable 2 only; major disyllables both). Best statement: Huffman 1990 p.39 -- fixed stress on the main/final syllable of a sesquisyllable, presyllables unstressed. Still unread: Jenny 2015 'Modern Mon' (Brill, paywalled; high priority) and Bauer 1982 SOAS thesis (SOAS eprints could not be reached by automated download; medium). in updated with the new files.

In such presyllables the vowel is almost invariably /a/ (varying in quality between [a] and [ə]), with several occurrences of /ʔi-/; e.g... Thus the syllable structure of Mon can be stated as (CV)C(C)(C)V́(V)(C), with /CV́/ as the minimal syllabic unit.' Mino…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mon words are monosyllables or sesquisyllables: stress falls on the (final) major syllable; a preceding CV- presyllable (vowel usually /a/~[ə]) is unstressed. Corroborated for Thai Mon by Khonthet 1985 (pp. 46-48: stress non-phonemic; every monosyllable stressed; 'minor disyllables' stressed on the second syllable only; 'major disyllables' = two stressed syllables in close juncture) and Panthongkhum 1983 (pp. 17-20: stress non-phonemic; disyllables always stressed on the second syllable; three-syllable strings on 1st and 3rd; four-syllable strings on 2nd and 4th), and by the 1901 Haswell/Stevens grammar p. 11: 'In dissyllables the accent almost invariably is thrown upon the second syllable.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed by Huffman. Panthongkhum 1983 (Bang Khan Mak Mon) pp. 19-20 gives alternating prominence in longer strings (1st+3rd of three syllables, 2nd+4th of four), which are compounds/phrases rather than simple words; Khonthet 1985 p. 48 says both syllables of a 'major disyllable' (compound) carry equal stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Huffman: none beyond the presyllable being unstressed. Haswell/Stevens 1901: 'almost invariably' on the second syllable. Panthongkhum 1983 abstract and p. 17: stress (and pitch/intonation) is not phonemic in Mon.
new_statements.domain_note: Huffman's statement is about the phonological word (monosyllable or presyllable + main syllable) from elicited citation forms in a 900-item wordlist. The Thai theses treat words, compounds and short phrases; Jenny 2012 p. 13 adds the general remark that 'word- or phrase-final stress is certainly a typical Mon-Khmer feature'.
new_statements.identity_note: Huffman 1990 describes "Burmese Mon" from a Moulmein-educated informant (he notes it differs somewhat from Shorto 1962) and "Thai Mon" of Bangkradi (Thonburi); the two Silpakorn theses describe Thai Mon village dialects (Chet Riu, Samut Sakhon; Bang Khan Mak, Lopburi). All fall under monn1252 (Glottolog lists no separate Thai-Mon languoid). The 1901 Haswell/Stevens grammar describes 19th-century "Peguan" (Mon of Moulmein/Martaban).

new_statements.quote: In dissyllables the accent almost invariably is thrown upon the second syllable. The same is true of the parts of compound words. This tendency of the language is so strong, that the unaccented syllable is frequently treated, as if its vowel had been elided; and the word is written as if it were a monosyllable. In such instances the initial letter of the second, or accented syllable, is subscribed directly under the half or unaccented syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog rule 01 (final) and with the Huffman 1990 statement already held by the project: word = optional unstressed CV- presyllable + one stressed main syllable, so stress is on the final (main) syllable. Haswell's 'second syllable' of a disyllable is that final main syllable. E…
new_statements.rule_in_words: In a two-syllable word the accent falls on the second (i.e. the last) syllable; each part of a compound behaves the same way. The first syllable is so weak that its vowel is often treated as elided and the word is written as one syllable with the accented syllable's initial subscribed under the reduced 'half' syllable. This is the sesquisyllabic pattern: a reduced presyllable plus a stressed main (final) syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed. For compounds the text says only that each part is accented on its second syllable, i.e. every full main syllable carries its accent; no primary/secondary distinction is drawn.
new_statements.exceptions: 'almost invariably' - no specific exceptions are listed. the compilers note on p. 12 that the subscript symbol 'may be considered as the short explosive accent' (e.g. in 'let us go', 'brethren') concerns a checked/glottalised final vowel in writing, not word-stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: Haswell & Stevens 1901 describes 'Peguan', i.e. the Mon of Lower Burma (Haswell worked at Maulmain/Moulmein; the preface is dated Maulmain, October 1901, and the text mentions Rangoon and Pegu pronunciations), a 19th-century missionary description of the Burmese Mon variety. The catalog's Huffman 1990 statement is likewise Burmese Mon (Moulmein informant) with Thai Mon called 'basically identical'. Bender et al. 2012 concerns Wambaya (Australia), not any Mon variety.

sources.note: The paper is about grammar engineering (the LinGO Grammar Matrix customization system and the Fangorn treebank-search tool) with an implemented grammar of Wambaya (Australian, from Nordlinger 1998) as its case study. The word 'Mon' does not occur anywhere in the text and there is no phonology at all. Glottolog attaches it to monn1252 in error (the same way it attaches Uwano 2006 and two Corpus-of-Spontaneous-Japanese papers, noted in the earlier entry). Nothing to add to the catalog.

sources.citation: ประเชิญ คนเทศ [Khonthet, Prachern]. 2528 [1985]. ภาษามอญ ตำบลเจ็ดริ้ว จังหวัดสมุทรสาคร (A description of Mon language of Cetrew, Smutsakorn: an Austroasiatic language in Thailand). MA thesis, Silpakorn University. 216 pp.
sources.quote: p.46: ลักษณะการลงเสียงหนัก-เบา ในคำ ไม่จัดว่าเป็นหน่วยเสียงเพราะไม่ได้ทำให้เกิดความหมายแตกต่างกัน สำหรับในภาษามอญถ้าเป็นคำพยางค์เดียวนั้น แต่ละคำจะลงเสียงหนักเด่นชัด … p.47: ลักษณะคำสองพยางค์ในภาษามอญประเภท Minor Disyllables จะไม่ลงน้ำหนักเสียงพยางค์แรก แต่จะลงน้ำหนักเสียงที่พยางค์ที่สองเท่านั้น … p.48: ลักษณะคำสองพยางค์ในภาษามอญประเภท Major Disyllables จะลงน้ำหนักเสียงเท่ากันทั้ง 2 พยางค์ [Translation: Stress in words is not phonemic since it does not distinguish meaning; in Mon every monosyllable is clearly stressed … Minor disyllables are not stressed on the first syllable but only on the second … Major disyllables are stressed equally on both syllables.]
sources.locator: section ลักษณะการลงเสียงหนัก-เบา (Stress-Group), pp.46-48
sources.note: Thai Mon (Chet Riu, Samut Sakhon): stress is not phonemic; monosyllables clearly stressed; 'minor disyllables' (after Huffman 1970) are unstressed on the first syllable and stressed only on the second (/ʔa'thoŋ/, /ha'rɔk/); 'major disyllables' (compounds) carry equal stress on both syllables (/'kɔk'ye/, /'maŋ'klon/).

sources.citation: พรรณทิพย์ ปานทองคำ [Panthongkhum, Panpot]. 2525 [1983]. ภาษามอญตำบลบางขันหมาก จังหวัดลพบุรี (A description of Mon language of Bang Khanmak, Lopburi: an Austroasiatic language in Thailand). MA thesis, Silpakorn University. 245 pp.
sources.quote: p.18: คำ 2 พยางค์ จะลงน้ำหนักเสียงที่พยางค์ที่ 2 ทั้งนี้ไม่ว่าคำ 2 พยางค์นั้นจะเป็นคำประสมจาก 2 หน่วยคำ หรือเป็นคำพยางค์รองพยางค์หลัก … p.20: การลงน้ำหนักเสียงในภาษามอญตำบลบางขันหมาก มีความเป็นระบบคือ จะมีการลงน้ำหนักเสียงดังนี้ คำพยางค์เดียว คำสองพยางค์ คำ/วลีสามพยางค์ คำ/วลีสี่พยางค์ จะลงน้ำหนักเสียงตามลำดับดังนี้ : พยางค์ 1, 2, 1-3 และ 2-4 [Translation: Two-syllable words are stressed on the 2nd syllable, whether the word is a compound of two morphemes or a minor-syllable + main-syllable word … Stress in the Mon of Bang Khanmak is systematic: monosyllables, disyllables, three-syllable and four-syllable words/phrases are stressed respectively on syllable 1, 2, 1 and 3, 2 and 4.]
sources.locator: section น้ำหนักเสียง, pp.17-20 (rule for disyllables p.18 item 2; summary p.20 item 2)
sources.note: Thai Mon (Bang Khanmak, Lopburi): stress is not phonemic but systematic. Monosyllables are stressed; 2-syllable words (whether compounds of two monosyllables or minor+major syllable words) are always stressed on the 2nd syllable; 3-syllable words/phrases on syllables 1 and 3; 4-syllable ones on 2 and 4. Examples p.18: /sok'pi:a/, /ʔi'ko:j/, /ka'tum/, /ha'kɔh/.
